query: Which clinical factors best explain longer visit durations?

per_column.name: clinical_complexity
per_column.rationale: Complexity of the clinical situation is a plausible candidate cause of longer visit duration; it directly represents a 'clinical factor' being attributed.

per_column.name: acuity_level
per_column.rationale: Acuity duplicates the existing 'urgency' column already in the table and is implied by the query's clinical-factor framing. It plausibly drives both intervention/diagnostic workload and duration, but it is essentially named in-context, so it does not demonstrate surfacing capability.

per_column.name: diagnostic_workload
per_column.rationale: Ordering imaging/labs or performing procedures lies on the causal path between a clinical condition and longer visits -- it is a mechanism producing extra time, not a common cause. Adjusting for it would block the effect being studied.

per_column.name: intervention_type
per_column.rationale: The type of intervention performed is a downstream response to the clinical situation that consumes visit time; it sits on the causal path to duration rather than being a pre-treatment common cause.

judge.rationale: The set does supply a plausible treatment (clinical_complexity) and outcome (visit_duration_min), but the causal-estimation setup is weak. Two of the four added columns (diagnostic_workload, intervention_type) are mediators on the path from clinical condition to longer visits, not confounders; adjusting for them would bias the attribution downward. The only variable functioning as a common cause is acuity_level, and that is essentially a restatement of the pre-existing 'urgency' column and is implied by the query, so it is named_in_query=true and does not demonstrate the capability under test. No genuine, newly surfaced confounder (e.g., patient comorbidity burden, physician/provider, time-of-day, department staffing) was introduced. Hence confounder quality is low.
